description: We are Templarios Team from Puerto Madryn, Patagonia. Agustín is a full-stack developer and programming teacher; Tincho brings creativity and storytelling. We are building Brasa, an interactive 3D web app that harmonizes MODIS and VIIRS fire hot spots into one consistent record, so anyone can explore how wildfires have changed in Patagonia. We'd love help from people with remote sensing, data science or visual design skills.
summary: Brasa is an interactive 3D web map that makes 26 years of NASA FIRMS fire hot spot data comparable and easy to explore. MODIS (since 2000) and VIIRS (since 2012) detect fires at different resolutions, so merging them creates a false jump in fire activity when VIIRS appears. Brasa harmonizes both sensors with a VIIRS-to-MODIS correction factor derived from their overlap period, producing one consistent monthly series from 2000 to today. It also computes monthly anomalies against the historical median to reveal truly exceptional months. Users can scrub a timeline, see hot spots as 3D hexagon columns over terrain, compare raw vs. harmonized data, explore an anomaly calendar and follow a guided tour of Patagonia, in English or Spanish. This matters because fire trends guide emergency management, insurance, conservation and education, and a sensor change should never be mistaken for a real change on the ground. Brasa is open source and runs in any browser.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Brasa turns NASA FIRMS active fire data into an interactive 3D map that anyone can explore. Its core contribution is harmonization: MODIS (2000-present) and VIIRS (2012-present) detect fires at different spatial resolutions, so VIIRS reports many more hot spots. Naively merging both creates an artificial jump in fire activity after 2012. Brasa corrects this so 26 years of data can be compared fairly.

HOW IT WORKS

1. Data pipeline (Python): we download historical MODIS and VIIRS archives plus near-real-time data from the FIRMS API, clean them, and aggregate detections by month and location.

2. Harmonization: using the overlap period where both sensors observed the same areas, we derive a VIIRS-to-MODIS scaling factor and express the full series on a common MODIS-equivalent scale.

3. Anomalies: for every month we compare activity against the historical median for that calendar month, separating truly exceptional events from normal seasonality.

4. Visualization: the processed data is served as static JSON and rendered in the browser as 3D hexagon columns over terrain. Height and color encode fire intensity.

FEATURES

- Month-by-month timeline from 2000 to today

- 3D hexagon map over real terrain, with dark and light basemaps

- Raw vs. harmonized comparison

- Anomaly calendar highlighting exceptional months

- Guided tour with a Patagonia (Chubut) case study

- Bilingual interface (English / Spanish)

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

Fire trend analysis informs emergency planning, insurance risk, conservation and environmental journalism. Brasa prevents a sensor change from being mistaken for a real change on the ground, and makes satellite data understandable for non-experts, students and decision makers. Future steps include regional alerts and automated risk reports.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGIES

TypeScript, Next.js 15, React, MapLibre GL, deck.gl (HexagonLayer), ECharts, Python for data processing, OpenFreeMap basemaps, open Terrarium elevation tiles, NASA FIRMS (MODIS and VIIRS), deployed on Vercel. Code hosted on GitHub.

CREATIVITY AND DESIGN CHOICES

We chose a 3D, game-like visual language to make a dry scientific dataset engaging, while keeping the method transparent through the raw vs. harmonized view and the guided tour. We considered data consistency across sensors, performance in the browser (precomputed static data, no backend required), accessibility for non-technical users, and openness: the project uses only public data and open source tools.
